speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, motion pictures have a profound cultural and economic effect on all Canadians. No one concerned about the preservation of Canadian culture can deny the influence of films on our attitudes and way of life in general. Since Canada is now the largest foreign market for United States films in the world, where for example 96 per cent of the feature films exhibited in Ontario are U.S. made and, considering that the distribution of motion pictures in Canada is largely American controlled, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. That this House urge the government to bring forward a film policy which will ensure the development and distribution of a viable and sustained production of Canadian films.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to seek the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the Anti-Inflation Board has rolled back the wage settlement of Local 6166 of the United Steel Workers of America in Thompson, Manitoba, to a point at which it is below the salaries earned by steel workers in Sudbury; in view of the fact that this decision not only contravenes a section of the Anti-Inflation Act which allows for wage parity within a sector but also creates difficulties in persuading people to accept work in Thompson, and in view of the fact that the government has the authority to over-rule a decision of the AIB on exactly those grounds, and has done so in the past, I move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt):
That this House instruct the cabinet to over-rule the Anti-Inflation Board on this issue and award Local 6166 of the Steel Workers of America a contract equal to that of steel workers in Sudbury.

ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-STATE OF TEXTILE INDUSTRY Mr. Jim Balfour (Regina East) moved:
That this House views with alarm the accelerating collapse of the Canadian textile industry, rejects the fatalistic inertia of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and demands serious action to counter the ruinous pressure from excessively high import levels.

Mr. Speaker, before touching upon the particular and central subject of this debate, namely, the Canadian textile industry, I think
Textile Industry
it is very timely that we discuss in this House this afternoon some of the things relating to the economy and the atmosphere created by the government vis-a-vis business in general.
It goes without saying that governments are not meant to represent big anything; they are meant to represent the people. That is almost a cliche. It is something we sometimes forget. Of course governments are not meant to represent big institutions, be they unions or big business.
I want to underline time and time again this afternoon that a government cannot and should not be the spokesman for any particular segment of society or the economy. Having said that, I want to state that the government has absolutely no excuse for what I call the degree of anti-business bias that it has shown under eight years of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), our former leader, mentioned in Nova Scotia some nights ago that the time for confrontation between major interests in society is over, and the time for conciliation is here. I agree. If anyone in this House thinks I am kidding about that, just go from one end of this country to the other and talk to businessmen. They will say that never in the last 40 years have they been given such a hostile reception as they have been given by this government.
Oh, oh!

Hon. members opposite do not like to hear the truth. It is going to take more than the seraphic smile of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) to rectify this situation. This anti-business bias and anti-business climate are even exaggerated in the case of the Canadian textile industry.

Mr. Speaker, what are we dealing with in the House today? We are discussing whether or not, in the near future, we shall have a textile industry in this country and I wish to state most emphatically that unless we do something right now, we shall not have any.

It has been said time and time again by businessmen in this country that business leaders and businessmen from other countries receive here in Ottawa a much more cordial and decent reception than our domestic businessmen. I think the minister will have to explain this. We have brought this motion before the House of Commons today purely and simply because we on this side of the House believe that if immediate action is not forthcoming, not just promises and words, much sooner than later we shall not have a Canadian textile industry.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke with several executives in the textile industry. In my view there is no cooperation in this area between the Ottawa officials and the industry which can compare with the kind of cooperation existing in the United States between Washington and the textile industry.
In Ottawa decisions are made without consultations with the private sector, with the industry. I do not wish to blame the minister in question all the time but his officials are often in the foreground and he is responsible. On many

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry
occasions, and I am sure many hon. members will agree with me, businessmen and textile manufacturers are informed by government officials that a decision has been made without any previous consultation.
I think it is very important to call attention to this state of affairs. For the last five or six years, as I have gone around the country, businessmen in the textile sector have been telling me they cannot understand the hostility shown to them by federal civil servants. It is almost as though they were not welcome here in Ottawa. I know the minister is not entirely to blame.
I want to say at the outset that I agree with much of the government's policy in connection with the textile industry. The fact is, however, that the policy we build up in the House of Commons is not carried out or, when it is carried out, it is too late-the damage has been done. This is a general consideration, one we should speak and think about in the House. I am not going to start being sensational, but I believe this is a problem which faces each and every one of us as parliamentarians, be we on the government side or on the opposition side. In the last year or so I have talked to many ministers who have told me privately that on many occasions the intentions of the bills and the orders we have drafted in the House of Commons have been completely controverted in subsequent regulations made by the bureaucrats-the whole intent of the law has been controverted by civil servants interpreting it in their own fashion or putting up roadblocks or, as in the case of the textile industry, failing to apply it. This applies to many policies which we have approved as legislators in the House of Commons. This being the case, as I believe it is, let us debate the issue openly because it is my opinion that in many instances the government has built up a monster in the form of a bureaucracy which nobody can control. [Translation]
As far as textile is concerned, I fully agree with the policy as a whole but, unfortunately, we are here to find an answer to a very serious problem for several members, especially members from Quebec. I would say that in general I totally agree with most of the government's policy but it should act responsibly, and it is not a policy which is implemented often enough by the officials concerned.

I would simply like to say this: I am very suspicious, after being around here for a few years-
Too long.
You are just a young fellow.

I am more than suspicious that some very influential officials and some cabinet ministers believe that the textile industry in Canada is expendable. They are not alone in this point of view. I have talked to businessmen in big cities, men who have nothing to do with the textile industry and who have never lived in textile towns, who say that the textile industry is expendable. That is the

conventional wisdom within much of the bureaucracy which has to apply textile policy.
The minister is a good minister in many ways. He is loyal to his civil servants, unlike some of his colleagues. But if he is really frank with the House he will admit he has run into this head-in-the-sand conventional wisdom that, for one reason or another, the textile industry in Canada is expendable. If this is what the minister is hearing from his advisers, whether in the private sector or in the public service, I think he should level with us because we are talking now about the survival of an industry which is important not only to Eastern Canada and to various other areas of the country, but to Canada as a whole. It is imperative that we find a good solution and a long term solution to the problems of a troubled industry.
In my view it would be disastrous to accept the conventional wisdom that somehow or other we can get along very well in this country without a textile industry. I want to make it abundantly clear that we in the Progressive Conservative party are committed to the existence of a viable textile industry here in Canada.
Hear, hear!

I can almost hear the minister saying, when he replies to the debate, "We, too, are committed to that objective." But, Mr. Speaker, ministers on the other side have been saying that for far too many years, and every year the situation has been getting worse and worse. I am not speaking only on behalf of the industry. I am speaking on behalf of all Canadians who want this industry to continue. Ministers whose responsibility this is will have to replace mere words with action and prove the sincerity of their undertaking. The industry does not need any more studies, commissions, reports, and committees of investigation. What the industry needs is a firm declaration from the government that there is a national will in favour of its continued existence, along with concrete measures which will bring some hope for the future.
I have always said that the federal government is shortsightedly living off the short-term windfall benefits resulting from the sale of our natural resources while letting in cheap imports. This is not to say, Mr. Speaker, that these imports will always be cheap. Once we have destroyed the means of Canadian production, what happens? One of the hon. members who sits opposite said to me the other day that he used to be able to go into a store and buy shirts, for instance, made in the Far East at a price far cheaper than anything we could match here, but that this situation was now coming to an end; the imported shirts were getting more and more expensive.
The government talks about the benefits the public derives from cheap imports. Mr. Speaker, those benefits are very short-lived. Take binder twine, for instance. We warned the government time and time again of what would happen if a domestic supply of binder twine were not available to farmers. People who should have known better allowed this industry to be destroyed by cheap imports, using the excuse that the farmer was benefiting from lower prices. What has happened? Only a year or so [DOT]after the local industry was destroyed the price has risen by three times.

Four.
June 16, 1976

I apply this situation, by analogy, to the textile industry. Consumers should not swallow the bait that they would be better off by getting short-term benefits. Quite apart from that, what happens when our natural resources run out? From what source can the government expect further windfall benefits to finance social programs?
The point is this: we have been saying, both inside and outside the House for a number of years, that the government has no industrial strategy. If we are wrong, then in the name of goodness will you tell the House what it is? Will you tell the businessmen about it because they are waiting to hear you? I do not intend to get mixed up in philosophy, in a discussion of the merits of private industry and free enterprise versus socialism, and so on; what I am asking is this: in the name of goodness tell us where you want business to go, because we don't know. I am not saying we want Mr. Howe or his ghost back. I am asking for some indication of a general industrial strategy for this country.

Mr. Speaker, I shall certainly correct my mistake, and I apologize once again.

I just want to underline in general the necessity for an industrial strategy for Canada, which is no more emphasized than by the situation in which the textile industry finds itself at the present time. I should like to make one last general remark before citing some global statistics vis-a-vis the textile industry. I have always felt that, unlike any other country that I know of, particularly in the western world, many of our senior bureaucrats and some ministers of the Crown think that the textile industry is expendable. They have this old-fashioned international trade philosophy, which I suggest is about 40 years out of date, that says "So long as you guys take our natural resources, some of our foodstuffs and our raw materials, to heck with the textile industry, it is expendable". I have heard that alluded to, being on the opposition side for so long, and I am sure the minister would like it to be prolonged.
We do not always get to talk with the senior bureaucrats as frankly as the minister does, but I am pretty darned sure that that is the advice he gets. It is a saw-off-"You take our natural resources, our foodstuffs and so on, and we will keep talking to the textile industry and try and keep them happy, though we really do not think they are viable". That is a disastrous situation.

speechtext: Yes, at meetings that you did not even attend.

I want to put a question to the hon. member because his intervention seems quite strange at this time. Did the hon. member talk with the union leaders, with the heads of companies? Are they satisfied with the present government's textile policy?

speechtext: That is not the question.

I agree, that is not the question. You have the answer and the best thing for you to do now is to keep quiet a little while.

There is also the question of the Third World countries. I am proud to be a Canadian, and I say that in a non-partisan way, in terms of our responsibilities in international trade and so on. There is nothing partisan about this. But there is another conventional wisdom which says that if we get tough in the textile sector we will be damaging the ability of the Third World countries to export. I have heard that debate. The fact is that Canada is doing one heck of a lot more than any other country in terms of permitting the Third World to be viable exporters, whether of textiles or any other materials.
I am not going to get into the general debate as to whether we are tough negotiators or not. I am as aware as any member of this House of the rightfully legitimate aspirations of emerging Third World countries, emerging not in the political sense but in the economic sense. But while we are leading the world in our understanding of this, I am sure that even the Third World countries do not want our textile industry to disappear completely, as it is beginning to do at this time. The reason we are debating this question today is that we on this side of the House firmly believe-

-that if immediate measures are not taken in the very near future, the textile industry will disappear.

Are we talking about completely sacrificing this traditional industry when we talk about our position in relation to the third world? This is nor an original statement of mine, but I will repeat it. Obviously what is needed is a rationalization of our approach. Some might say, what does the word "rationalization" mean?

speechtext: I have asked for more than that and the House agreed. If the hon. member wants to limit himself to 10 minutes, that is his own decision.

To those officials and others who declare the conventional wisdom that the textile industry is expendable, to those in their ivory towers who have never visited a textile town, I am going to say this. I realize that the textile industry is spread across Canada in every province. But in my own part of Canada when you talk of a textile town you are talking of a one industry town. These are towns with a population of 12,000, 15,000, 25,000 people. Very often a large primary textile plant is the only employer. Do not ask me why. Sometimes these towns have industrial commissaires, as we say in French, but they never have any industry in addition to the textile industry. Up until recently labour has not been generously paid; les salaires ne sont pas fameux. Especially the older workers lack mobility. In human terms and in terms of suffering, it is not just ordinary unemployment that hits a textile town; it is devastating unemployment, grinding unemployment, unemployment of the worst kind.
These workers not only lack mobility, Mr. Speaker, especially if they have been working until they are 45 or 55 years of age and then have to find work somewhere else. Apart from the fundamental consideration that any country with a secondary industrial base, such as Canada, must have a viable textile industry, I appeal to those-and I declare there are many-who say that the textile industry is expendable to reconsider their point of view, and I ask them to visit towns not only in Quebec but all over Canada that depend on this one industry.
If the United States government had let happen in the U.S. what we are now letting happen in Canada, the United States textile industry would have disappeared over five years ago. Domestic consumption in Canada accounts for about 46 per cent of textile output, extending to approximately 200,000 jobs. Compare this with Japan where 90 per cent of the industry is domestic. I have already alluded to the United States. Eighty per cent of the consumption of textiles in the United States is of goods from the domestic industry, as is the case in many of the EEC countries. As I am sure many hon. members are aware, this is accomplished through quotas instead of by tariffs. If we can hold our own with the EEC and the United States there would be a minimum of 150,000 more jobs created in Canada. This is not going to be easy. There are 200,000 jobs involved in making the textiles imported into Canada from abroad, and I suggest that 150,000 domes-

tic jobs could be created because of the superior productivity of Canadian textile manufacturing.
The Canadian textile trade represents 1 per cent of the world-wide market or, as I said before, 200,000 jobs, and imports represent 54 per cent. That is, there are 200,000 jobs approximately in other countries, and I have already alluded to the increased productivity in Canada, so that we stand a good chance of creating 150,000 more jobs here in our own country. Canada's consumption is 2 per cent of world consumption, whereas manufacturing represents 1 per cent of world production.
Having listened, not only to industrial spokesmen, but to many others including union spokesmen, it is my view that if we froze imports we could bring production up to a satisfactory level. That would not mean we would diminish the status quo of the Third World countries. It would probably take four years to get production up to the level of 80 per cent of the domestic market by Canadian manufacturers.
As I said before, the United States has comprehensive quotas from yarn to finished product, and I believe this is what the Canadian industry vitally wants. It is the domestic industry which keeps prices low. If we lose the viable domestic industry, and I have already made the argument in respect of the binder twine situation regarding agricultural products, then prices may well skyrocket. This is arguable but not so arguable as prices are now; however, if we eliminate domestic competition I suggest prices will skyrocket.
Trade agreement rules are the same for the United States, Canada, and many other countries. As I have said time and time again-

-and at the beginning of my remarks, the rules as applied in other countries are not applied by the civil servants here in Canada.

Of countries that are rapidly developing, only Canada is short-term in its outlook in that we do not have comprehensive tariffs, although I have argued this afternoon basically for the quota approach. The suggestion is to freeze the basic quota on imports, and the domestic percentage of production increase will be Canadian without affecting the status quo of Third World imports. Quotas should conform to the average of U.S. and EEC quotas.
The Canadian textile industry is advocating a quota policy similar to that of the United States instead of placing the emphasis on tariffs. Foreign imports would not be cut back, but instead would be frozen until Canadians regained a share of their market equal to the United States control of its domestic market. When this occurred this freeze on imports would be replaced with a quota system which would be kept on par, with U.S. quotas.
It is fair to say that we are talking about a four-year period or something in that general time frame. I think it is also fair to say that Third World countries would understand the rational approach we are taking in this regard.
Before moving the motion, and I think from what you have said, Mr. Speaker, I might have some difficulty in

that regard, but we will cross that bridge when we come to it-
It has already been moved.

Mr. Speaker, I am very fortunate when it comes to the rules in being not too far away from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
The Standing Committee of the Senate on Banking, Trade and Commerce was seized of many problems concerning the Canadian textile industry. Before moving the motion I would like to put on record some-
At least you are consistent.

I would like to put on record some of the more salient points that were touched upon there. The minister is already aware of them, but I think they should be headlined.
In spite of increasing textile and clothing exports the Canadian negative trade balance has grown by an average annual rate of 16 per cent since 1969, and had reached $1.1 billion by 1974. This is not only a serious matter for the textile industry; we on this side of the House suggest it is a serious matter also for Canada. I have already referred to the delays that take place in implementing decisions, and I note here the lengthy and damaging procedural delays which often follow the completion of any inquiry of the Textile Clothing Board. We know that in nine separate cases four months lapsed between the time the board's reports were submitted to the minister and the date when the reports were tabled and made public.
We often hear, and I think very unfairly, that the domestic industry in Canada does not have a good rate of productivity. Let me point out simply that, compared to other countries, and I have already underlined this in terms of job creation, productivity is pretty good. Let us consider comparative statistics here in Canada. Productivity in the textile industry has increased over the past decade at an average rate of 5.1 per cent compared with 4.2 per cent for all manufacturing. I think that is a pretty good record. Let me say to all those critics who suggest that some parts of our textile industry are obsolete, they are obsolete in many instances because the industry will not invest in new, modern plants until it gets some long-term direction from the federal government.
In addition to problems created in the industry by delays and the lack of vigorous administration of textile policy, there are many elements of the policy itself which militate against its stated objective, that is, to provide a sense of direction and a framework and conditions within which the textile and clothing industry can plan and invest with a greater degree of confidence.
Finally, another element of the policy, or lack of it, which has adversely affected the whole industry relates to the required climate of confidence and stability and the necessity of the board to recommend immediate removal of restraint measures or to refrain from recommending new measures on the basis of short-term marketing considerations. I think anyone who recognizes the working of the appeal board and the delays in the short-term considerations recognizes what an important matter this is.
Textile Industry
In closing I would say it is apparent to us on this side of the House that the Canadian textile industry is in serious danger. We brought this debate on this afternoon because we believe that unless we have no more commissions, no more studies, no more of this and that, but instead immediate action, the industry will be in greater danger.
I sympathize with the minister because he will have to come down pretty hard on a lot of senior officials who will say to him behind closed doors, "We are expendable, and many of these things will have to go down the drain before we can export this, that, and the other thing." I hope the minister will level with us and give the country in general, and the textile industry in particular, a strategy of hope for the future.

For the reasons I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, I cannot move this motion. Would you enlighten me, Mr. Speaker? Frankly and sincerely, I find the situation rather complex. May I second .. . but the motion is already seconded-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The motion has already been moved. Notice appeared on the Order Paper and the motion was moved by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Balfour) and seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). The hon. member was just speaking on the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you ever so much for your very kind assistance. Under the circumstances, obviously the only thing for me to do at the end of my three speeches is to ask the House to support our motion.

Mr. Speaker, even though the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) did not move the motion I should like to congratulate him for his good intentions. I certainly also wish to express my admiration for his passion regarding the position of the textile industry. I think this does him a great deal of credit. Nevertheless, I think I would be less than frank if I did not say that I found some of his remarks somewhat too simple in the sense that they did not answer the questions. While I can understand the deep emotion behind his concern about the industry, the situation is not as straightforward as he would put it, nor do we have any really clear indication what the Conservative party would be prepared to do officially in this regard.
When the hon. member says that he wants quotas put on and wants to lower imports from other countries completely over a period of years, I can understand that as it affects Canadian workers. However, I cannot understand it as it concerns our international responsibilities. Surely the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, who is well known in this House of Commons for his sentiments regarding assistance to countries around the world, is not serious when he says that Canada should stop all imports from other countries, if I understood him correctly, or place an immediate quota on them until the industry revives, and then when the industry revives, establish some high level of import quota.

I did not say that.

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry

The other thing he did not make very clear is whether his party is a high tariff party and whether it wants to see the tariff increased. There is in fact a very considerable tariff on textiles now. I fail to understand his argument when he says that if there were no foreign textile industry Canadian prices of textiles would be higher than they are now. In fact the reason we have some of the highest textile prices in the world is the protection given to the textile industry in Canada, as inadequate as the hon. member may think it is.
The point is that the consumers of Canada are clearly being asked to pay higher prices for the goods they consume in order to protect a vital industry in this country. The question is to what extent can we bring up the level of protection, and to what extent does his party officially stand as a high protection party, and is his leader prepared to go back to Alberta, or to any of the other western provinces which historically have had a grievance with Quebec and Ontario, where the textile industry is located, and where the people have said that they have had to pay through the nose in order to provide jobs in Ontario and Quebec when they could have bought this type of goods at a much lower price, and advocate that?
I think it is grossly unfair for the hon. member in this kind of a situation to say that he thinks there is a problem. In some ways I think this motion misses what is the core of the problem, not only in the textile industry but in other industries as well. I agree with the hon. member when he says that the absence of an industrial strategy is one of the problems. The government never has developed an industrial strategy or, if it has, it has been a piecemeal policy that is squeezed out of it from time to time by accident. Nor do I understand why the hon. member for Brome-Mis-sisquoi would take off on the personnel of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The fault lies squarely with the government. A government is responsible for policy.
Why is it that whenever anything goes wrong the Conservative party always places the blame not where is squarely belongs on those who have authority but rather on the public servants. The public servants take orders from the minister and the government who are responsible for policy. If there is something wrong with textile policy they should blame the government and the minister if they wish, but they should not blame the public servants who will do whatever the government tells them to do.
Surely the hon. member is not telling us that if his party were to form the government they would not be able to do anything because public servants would prevent them doing it, or that they would have to have wholesale layoffs of public servants in order to have a textile policy. Surely that is not the case.
I think the most serious reason we have this great present difficulty in the textile industry is the high level of unemployment. When you have 7.4 per cent to 7.5 per cent of the population unemployed no one can think straight about what should be done in terms of our responsibilities to our own people as against our responsibilities internationally. Everyone starts looking inwards and tries to protect every single job. That is very understandable. The point is that there can be no solution for the textile industry or any other worthy industry so long as 7.4 per cent of

the people are unemployed, because then the first priority of every member of this House becomes one of getting people back to work and ensuring jobs for the future. The danger is that jobs may be found to our detriment as a country living among other countries in terms of our own responsibilities to other people.
While we have problems in this country and must consider those problems, I do not think our problems are of such a nature that we have to turn our backs on the rest of the world and say Canada will become protectionist and that what happens in other countries is just too bad, that charity begins at home. Therefore it seems to me that the first priority must be full employment in order to get the textile industry going again. Only under conditions of full employment can any rationalization of industry take place. I have been a person who has looked at this industry over many years. The industry has been in trouble as long as I can remember. There has been one trouble or another. When we have a high level of unemployment such as exists now, then of course demand is low in the country and the purchasing power is not there to pick up a lot of the output. But the industry was in trouble as well when we had a fuller level of employment.
It was not so many years ago that representations were being made to members of parliament to open the flood gates of immigration in order to feed the textile industry of Canada because it could not get people to work in the industry. The point is that under full employment, as difficult as that may be, what happens is that change can take place. When you have full employment, when there are alternate jobs, people can move between industries. The industry can rationalize itself. It knows that there is consumer purchasing power.
What has happened is that some of our textile firms have done very well. They have upgraded their products; they have adjusted the kind of products they make to the high style market and to the ^dnds of things that do not have to compete with the low wage countries or the mass-produced textiles which can be produced in other countries around the world. They have adjusted, but they have done that under conditions of full employment.
The other concern I have about the speaker who preceded me is that the whole tone of his speech up until the very end was one of concern about investment in the industry, about the employer in the industry. We in this House of Commons must be concerned about everyone. I start from a somewhat different premise. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi I guess was saying that what is good for employers is good for the workers. I have come to another conclusion, that what is good for the workers has to be good for the employers because workers are far more numerous than employers and are less able to look after themselves or adapt to employers.
Under conditions of full employment workers in the textile industry have a number of choices they can make. They can be retrained or they can go to other jobs. Because industry is changing they can find employment, and there is a much better future for them and often for their employers as well. It is a disgrace in this country, and I blame the government for it, not the public servants of this
June 16, 1976

country-I blame the policy makers of this country for the state of our manufacturing industry.
In this morning's Globe and Mail there is an article by Wayne Cheveldayoff in which he lists the deficit in our manufacturing industry. He writes:
Last year, Canada imported $9.8 billion more of manufactured, inedible end products than it exported-more than double the $4.5 billion deficit of 1972.
Part of that, of course, was textiles but all of it was end products, the kind of things that provide jobs in this country. I agree with the mover, or rather the non-mover of the motion, that the government has traded off raw material irreplaceable exports for jobs in Canada. This was just as true when the Conservatives were in office as when the Liberals were in office. They could never make up their minds whether they wanted Canada to be an exporter of raw materials or to develop its secondary manufacturing industry. They were going to please everyone, but the point is that you cannot please everyone and the evidence is quite clear.
To the extent that we export raw, unfinished goods, we have to import something in exchange. You cannot go on exporting without importing. What is there to bring back? We do not need raw, unfinished goods, so we bring back manufactured goods such as textiles, but textiles form a relatively small dollar part of the sum of $10 billion. What we are doing in fact is exporting jobs when we export raw materials. That is the kind of thing over which the bureaucrats do not have any control. That is a policy decision of the government, or the absence of any policy decision in terms of an industrial strategy, and that is what causes our problem.
The effect of continuing the export of raw materials is to raise the value of the Canadian dollar, especially when on top of exporting raw materials we start raising a hue and cry about the vast amount of capital we have to import into this country in order to build things like the Mackenzie pipeline and other kinds of high capital intensive units such as opening new mines and establishing the infrastructure associated with mines. You cannot create jobs that way. The effect of importing capital is to raise the value of the Canadian dollar, and as that happens it destroys the competitiveness of Canadian secondary industry and it creates a high level of unemployment in this country.
I think it is important when we deal with a subject of this kind to lay the blame where it belongs. We call for the appropriate solution, which must be a policy of full employment. The government has obviously turned down that solution as evidenced in its last budget when it is quite prepared to accept 7.4 per cent unemployment in the country. Difficult as it is for the textile industry, it will be equally difficult for every other manufacturing industry in the country. I think the government must stand condemned for its failure to bring in an industrial strategy, its failure to understand the economy of this country, and if it does understand it it must stand condemned for not acting in terms of its budgetary measures to reduce unemployment in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I also wish to thank the sponsor of today's motion which relates
Textile Industry
to the textile industry and is extremely important, as was said earlier, particularly for Quebec and Ontario. Everyone knows the great importance of this industry for the economy of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario as well as other parts of the country.
As everybody knows, textiles are essential to the life of a modern people. Is it any wonder that Canadians are among the largest users of textile in the world? Annual purchases of textiles in Canada average in excess of 33 pounds per capita. Canada comes second after the United States for the average textile consumption. Canadian textile plants are located, as I just said, in industrial parts of Quebec and Ontario, close to the large urban markets. More than 80,000 Canadians, that is 6 per cent of the entire manufacturing labour in our country works in the textile industry. Every job in the manufacturing sector creates employment for 1.17 other people in the service, maintenance and repair sectors.
Therefore, the textile industry gives employment to more than 175,000 people who themselves support families, which adds up to over half a million people. The annual production exceeded $1.8 billion last year and the industry is 80 per cent Canadian-owned, which is quite important when one considers that any mature country must have its own textile supplies.
Mr. Speaker, these figures are extremely interesting and show how important the textile industry is in Canada. On the other hand, this industry is not a new one. In Canada, during the forties and the fifties, the primary textile and clothing industry came first as regards the number of jobs provided. In 1972, however, it fell to third place and primary textile plays a crucial part in regional development, particularly in Quebec. The textile industry is typical in that it employs mainly a large number of women. This industry, as I just said, is 80 per cent Canadian-owned.
And in the paper published in the February, 1976 issue of the Canadian Textile Journal, statistics and solutions are suggested which, I am sure, the officials in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce have or should have taken into consideration. To this date, we have not seen any recommendation from the federal government taking up the suggestions made by the textile industry itself. Whenever you make recommendations to this House, you are told it has not been proved right. It has been said that there were contradictions in the requests filed by certain manufacturers.
And yet, after having read the briefs submitted by the Textile Manufacturers Association, we have still not seen any government action involving the textile industry. Again this week, I asked a question of the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) on a similar industry, the footwear industry. He answered that the only recommendation he had made was first to ask the Minister of National Revenue to make inquiries under the Anti-Dumping Act. Inquiries made under the Anti-Dumping Act will not now solve the problem of the textile and footwear industries.
His second suggestion was he hoped the footwear industry would fall under the jurisdiction of the textile industry. Now, the February 1976 issue of the Canadian Textile

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry
paper said the Textile Board was not as efficient as we believed it would be when it was established. According to the textile industry, it seems to be bogged down in bureaucracy. We have serious ground to believe that, to raise questions and to put some to both levels of government. The Canadian Textile industry is not the only one to blame for a reduced production, because the provincial government and the federal government especially cannot escape their responsibilities. They have an important part to play in promoting development and growth in the textile industry through better control of imports.
This is becoming increasingly important, especially in view of the fact that while the textile trade deficit was $347 million in 1964, it had reached $918 million in 1973. This means that during the 10-year period, the deficit increased 165 percent. The question arises whether some other industries favoured imports to that extent, and which. However, the Canadian textile industry maintained its activities at the best possible level of efficiency. Capital investments by the industry during that 10-year period totalled $1.5 billion. However, it is unthinkable that any industrialized country would accept to import over 50 percent of its requirements, but unfortunately this is what is happening. It is also unthinkable that any industrialized nation should accept to import over 50 per cent of a basic product as essential as textiles. We have experienced a substantial growth in Canadian consumption in terms of pounds per capita.
The Canadian textile industry offers wages and conditions comparable with the best in the world for that industry. In Canada, a worker gets two weeks' pay after one year of service, compared to one week in the United States. On top of that, the Canadian worker gets 10 paid statutory and other holidays each year, while six only are provided in the United States. I say all this to prove that the textile industry is an old industry in Canada, a basic industry, a specialized industry, and that manufacturers are competent, that they have properly administered their industry. Nevertheless imports are their most dangerous enemy.
Here I am going to be told that we cannot avoid imports, that because of the standard of living in other countries, products which cost less in western countries must be allowed to come in and that we cannot prevent the Canadian people from buying less expensive products when they can be imported. We have here, Mr. Speaker, problem of political economy. We have here a problem of dollars and cents. The result is that, if we are to keep our industry in Canada so as to be our own masters in our own house, as we said on many occasions and particularly as the Liberal government opposite did at the last election, by investing at home and having our industries here, we must have a protectionist policy, and we must have protectionist without penalizing the Canadian people. This means that we must protect both our industries and the consumer. But we cannot protect the consumer because the salaries we have to pay make it impossible for us to produce as cheaply as eastern countries which are able to export textile into Canada because even the raw material in cheaper overthere than here because of the differences in living standards and labour cost. Therefore since we cannot compete with those countries we must protect our own industry and adopt protectionnist trade policies and we must also have a protection policy for the consumer and his purchasing

power, otherwise there is no way out. We shall always be submerged, flooded with those foreign products which we could very well manufacture ourselves. Instead of producing textile, footwear, furniture and other essential products, we shall see our skilled workers, our experts and manufacturers unemployed or bankrupt. As for those people who will be unemployed, we shall have to give them welfare and unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot solve the problem solely by regulating imports. We must have commercial and economic policies which give individuals and consumers the required purchasing power to buy domestic products according to the standard of living and salary conditions that exist in Canada. Mr. Speaker, this economic system would allow us to balance purchasing power, prices and our production capacity. We shall never be able to compete against other countries. This minister, like his predecessor, who is now president of the Anti-Inflation Board, did not solve anything by creating a Textile Board.
Absolutely nothing has been solved and now the same thing is offered as a solution to the problems of the Canadian footwear industry. This is what shoe manufacturers have asked, but for my part, I have absolutely no confidence in a board which was unable to solve from an economic view point the textile situation in Canada and which will be now asked to solve the problems of the footwear industry in Quebec and the rest of our country. This board, which was unable to solve the problems of the textile industry, will not be able to solve those of the footwear industry.
Canadian shoe manufacturers have in good faith asked the government in their brief submitted in February, that the Textile Board control or supervise the footwear industry. Those manufacturers may not then have realized that the Textile Board, like all other boards unfortunately is a sham established to convince the peopel that the problem will finally be examined, that solutions will be found and that the problem will be dealth with. And that does not happen.
They spend time, they spend money, they exchange correspondence, the minister tells the House he will urge the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) to look into the Anti-dumping Act with regard to cheap imports. But for months and years we have been hearing in this House Ministers of Industry, Trade and Commerce repeating the same tune. And each week we see industries that have to go out of business.
As the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Graff-tey) said a moment ago, in my riding and his in particular, an industry with hundreds and hundreds of employees has recently been forced to wrap up its operation; I am talking about Brock Mills. It was a prosperous, well managed industry which had proven its merit, which produced good quality and which was exporting throughout the world. Well, now, that industry, because of the department's inertia in the field of textile as in other fields-they always hide behind excuses such as our international trade-has been forced out of business. The government takes refuge, it always hides behind the problem of our imports.
June 16, 1976

Mr. Speaker, as long as the government will rely on imports from other countries to provide Canada with the necessary products and to satisfy the Canadian consumer, either our imports will cost millions and billions of dollars or our unemployment and social welfare measures will cost millions and billions of dollars. We cannot indefinitely come up with the excuse of external trade to solve the problem of the textile, footwear, clothing, and furniture industries and those of the other basic industries in Canada. We must have an economic policy which could help balance the national purchasing power of Canadians with the total of prices.
We must also have a protectionist policy for the Canadian consumers, producers, employees and employers, otherwise we won't find any solution. Tomorrow, Japan will not be our main competitor in textile, it will be another country. The day after tomorrow, again it will be another country which does not have the same standard of living, the same working conditions, the same salaries, which does not live like us, Canadians; however, we are obliged to have idle labour or people who live on welfare benefits even if they are experts, even if until now they have made a living in some basic industry in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the government could say; give us the solutions. We offered some time and time again to finance ministers and to industry and trade ministers, but they do not take them into account. Why should we waste our time giving solutions to this government which does not want to know anything, which does not want to hear anything and which relies only on its bureaucracy.
We can only criticize the government. Why? Because it does not want to hear about solutions. They seem to think that the solution is only within the Liberal party. Only the Liberals have received the light from the Holy Spirit and only they can rule the country. In spite of all the solutions we propose in the House, nobody listens to us. The solutions put forward by members of Parliament are not taken into account any more than those put forward by Canadian manufacturers in the footwear, textile, clothing or other basic industries. They are laughed at. For example, the same problem occurred recently in the agricultural field.
Bureaucrats run our administration and, unfortunately, our ministers in the House only repeat aloud what the bureaucrats think. I am sorry, I hate to say this to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) whom I consider as a nice guy, as someone who gives answers in the House, but, on the other hand, I think that the bureaucrats hiding behind the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce do not advise him as they should. I also regret, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as a minister tries to "shake his officials, his bureaucrats and his technocrats and begins to assert himself, he is transferred to another department.
As soon as a minister begins to take control of his department, to know his way around and to assert himself in order to find worthwhile solutions, unfortunately he is transferred to another department, and we are back to square one. When I see a cabinet shuffle, I am sad because I feel the minister being transferred was just about to find the proper answers. Would it be because he has become too troublesome, too much of a nuisance for his officials that
Textile Industry
he has to be transferred? I am getting very suspicious, Mr. Speaker.
We only have to read the numerous briefs submitted to us to find, for instance, that the Canadian footwear industry lost 46 per cent of its domestic market. During the first six months of this year, Canadian manufacturers shipped 23,158,000 pairs of shoes, or 46 per cent of all shipments on the Canadian market, while imports accounted for 27,628,000 pairs, or 54 per cent of the market.
Mr. Speaker, those figures were given to us by the industry, by those who made that footwear. The brief was presented to the Canadian Committee on Tariff and Trade on October 10, 1975. At the end of the brief, on finds the recommendations or conclusions put forward to the various departments and, in this case, to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Still, those solutions are not to be found in the act. They are no longer acknowledged, nowhere to be found. That means that they are not taken into account, that the arguing and "fooling around" continues in the system that had been set up.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I have to speak in this fashion. We are aware of the difficulties our domestic industries are experiencing, we know that every year people come to us out of concern when they realize the industry is decreasing its output by 25, 30 or even 40 per cent. Those people wonder, at 40 or 45 years of age, where, after having worked in the textile industry for 20 or 25 years, they can find a new job when that industry has to fold up.
Those are the problems put to us, the representations made to us by our constituents and we must take them into account. That is why I say that, if we had praise and congratulations to offer the minister, we would be happy to do so. On the other hand, as we have to bear the pressures of the public, of the people who earn their living in the footwear industry, on the employees and employers whose livelihood depends on that industry, we are forced to bring those matters to the attention of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who is responsible for the situation. However, I do hope we will not have to wait ten years till this is achieved, and that the minister will take whatever means are necessary to remedy the situation in an industry that is extremely important to Canada and especially to eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can undertand to some degree the confusion on the part of hon. members opposite as to who was the mover of the motion before the House, since I think the language is more that of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) than that of the hon. member under whose name the motion appears. I know there are many humorous stories about "politicians viewing with alarm," but I never thought I would see this language included in a motion moved in this House. In case hon. members have not noted the excessive language in the motion, may I read it to them? It says:
That this House views with alarm the accelerating collapse of the Canadian textile industry, rejects the fatalistic inertia of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and demands serious action to counter the ruinous pressure from excessive high import levels.
It would be hard to include in that kind of motion many more spectacular words.

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I wish I had said it.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am glad this motion was moved, because it gives me the opportunity to say some things about the textile industry.
First, of course, the textile industry is a problem sector of the Canadian industrial economy. After listening to hon. members opposite-indeed, I suppose to many people on this side-one might get the impression that this is the only country in the world in which the textile industry is in difficulty; whereas I know, from my travels, that the industry is in great difficulty in all industrialized countries, and in some less developed countries as well. What we have heard today has been, for the most part, largely a repetition of the sorts of things which have been said about the industry for many years. I think it is fair to say that, by and large, they are generalizations.
With the greatest of respect for the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, whose speech I enjoyed immensely, as I always do, he used "textiles" as an all-embracing, all-encompassing word, as if only a single commodity were involved; whereas the textile industry is made up of many different sectors.
The whole thing is sick.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member suggests that the whole industry is sick. I do not know where his shirt was made; probably it was made in Taiwan.
The industry is your responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not mind if hon. members want a little sparring match, but I wanted to be serious and give hon. members some information. I hope hon. members will do me the courtesy of allowing me to make my remarks.
We are waiting.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As I was saying, the textile industry is complex and involves many different sectors, some of which are frequently at odds with each other. I am thinking, for example, of the basic material aspect of the business as opposed to the finished goods aspect. I hope in the time that I have to demonstrate where quite frequently these can be at odds and can make it even more difficult to devise a comprehensive and all-embracing policy.
Let me first put to rest something which the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi said or suggested, that is that in some way or another there is a view in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce that this industry, and I think I use the word he used, is expendable. The simple truth is that that is not so. He asked me to level with him and the House.
I can say that I do not recall a single instance in which anybody has made that point. I might say that is one of the documents at which I was looking, there is a clear-cut comment by the department that a viable textile industry is an important sector for Canada and that it is a large employer. It confirms in fact something which the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi said, namely, that they are an employer of a particular type of worker for whom it is

not always easy to obtain alternative employment. For that reason it is even more important for it to be kept in as good a shape as possible.
Statistics that have been thrown around in this debate can be read in many different ways. However, I hope that some I quote will give a rough idea that things are not as bad over the whole industry as has been said. Nor are we as much the victims of imports as has been suggested.
For example, in the total textile market, that is, primary and made up goods, and I make that distinction because it is important, in dollar terms, domestic producer shipments amounted to 77.6 per cent of the total market for 1975. In dollar terms, of total textile imports, and this is an important point, 72 per cent came from industrialized countries and only about 20 per cent from low cost countries. That is something that very frequently gets overlooked.
We tend to assume that the problems of the textile industry are because of large imports from some of the so-called low cost countries. In fact the biggest country from which we import and the largest quantities is the United States, followed by some of the countries in Europe. I make that point because it indicates that the idea of tariffs, or even of quotas in the conventional sense'of the word, is not really going to be all that much help in terms of the United States market. For example, in recent weeks a good deal has been said about certain kinds of polyester yarn coming in from the United States. It has been suggested that this has obviously been harmful to the Canadian industry and, in fact, that there might be dumping involved. The truth is that there is no evidence of this. In fact it is primarily because the polyester market in the United States is soft. Therefore prices have come down in that country.
This brings up a continuing problem in this industry. That is the fact that styles, fashions, and public demands change. In this particular case there has been a dramatic decline in the popularity of the double knit market in terms of fashions. There are other members of the House who might be better able than I to comment on this. This has had a very traumatic effect in terms of that aspect of the industry.
There are three factors that exercise the greatest impact on the structure of the textile industry. I should like to address myself to one of these because it relates to something which the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi said, namely, the size of the domestic market. Part of the difficulty we have in this industry, as in many others, is the relatively small domestic base on which we have to work by comparison with, for example, the United States or some of the larger areas such as the European Economic Community, or Japan. In other words, we do not have that very big domestic market on which to draw. This gives us problems in the textile industry in terms of scale and also in terms of the range of the demand of the public.
In Canada we cannot produce the whole range of textile products, apparel, and related items because of our comparatively small domestic base. This is one problem that is related to the question I mentioned a moment ago, that is, that consumers desire variety which tends to fragment the production line and makes it much more costly.
June 16, 1976

Somebody in the textile industry said to me the other day in one of my meetings that if you stood at the corner of St. Catherine and Peel in Montreal for the whole day, you probably would not find two ladies going by with exactly the same kind of dress or same pattern of dress. That gives some indication of how broad the range is that has to be produced. I repeat, since it is a relatively small base on which they have to work, it adds to their costs.
I already mentioned the proximity of the United States. Incidentally, in comparing the Canadian textile industry with its counterpart in the United States, and I have said this before, there is some validity in the examination. It can also be misleading since the economies of scale which I mentioned allow the United States to get better production runs and better costs.
In this connection it is interesting to note some of the references that were made only recently by one of the largest unions involved in the textile industry. I would like to quote from it because I think it is a carefully thought out study. The union is the Centrale des Syndicats Demo-cratiques, the CSD. It recently presented a highly professional analysis which I recommend to hon. members who have a special interest in this subject. I quote from the study:
Imports are the scapegoat of this industry. We do not mean to say that their importance is negligible-we have already noted the increasing part of the Canadian market which they are securing-but rather that, even if the domestic market were completely monopolized by Canadian producers, the rate of expansion in textile industry would still not be comparable to that of the key industries. As we said earlier, the decline in this sector is partly due to its very nature (i.e., the weak revenue elasticity of the demand for its products).
In the same report there is a reference to comparisons with other countries and the base in terms of how we protect our industry versus other countries. Here they quote the industry spokesmen:
Textile imports, they maintain, are respectively $10, $22 and $9 per capita in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Community, whereas they are $30 in Canada in 1969-70.
This may have changed somewhat since that time, but probably not significantly.
According to these figures, Canadian producers seem to have relatively little protection against foreign competitors.
That is the impression given by the statistic.
In fact, the situation is quite different. Per capita imports in no way indicate the degree of protection; these figures are based essentially on two factors: the size of the country and the relative cost of production of textile fabrics in each country. The size of the country determines its reliance on the outside world;
That is what I was commenting on a moment ago.
-the larger the country, the lower the figure for per capita imports ... If these comparisons are limited to countries similar in size to Canada, Canadian textile producers seem well protected, per capita textile imports being respectively $78, $63 and $69 in Holland, Belgium and Sweden,-
These are countries of smaller populations, relatively speaking, than ours, but in the same general range. Therefore the suggestion that we are less protective is not borne out by the facts or statistics.
Also there is some real question as to whether short of total abolition of imports, you can carry out the protective mechanisms in terms of textiles very much beyond what we are doing at the present time without increasing costs,
Textile Industry
as the hon. member said would happen if we let the textile industry die. The same would probably apply if we put on very heavy tariff protections beyond what we have now. When all is said and done, we are going to need and will continue to need considerable fabrics from offshore.
I mention here what I referred to in my earlier remarks, namely, the difficulty between the finished goods manufacturer and the primary goods manufacturer. Obviously in most instances the finished goods manufacturer wishes to get his materials from as wide a range of resources as possible. He likes to have in large part an assured domestic supply, and at the same time to be able to draw on offshore markets.
One of the reasons for continuing studies, and I agree with the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi that they can go on interminably, but unfortunately are necessary, is that we have to get the apparel people and the primary production people together to try to figure out if we are going to go to a global quota system, as has been recommended, and how this would work in a satisfactory way for both sectors and for that whole range of products.
As I mentioned earlier, the industry is not in as bad a shape as some of the worst "doom and gloom" commentators suggest. The fact is that a recovery is now under way in several sectors. Other sectors are, as I mentioned, in real difficulty; nobody quarrels with that statement, and we are considering what additional steps may be necessary, particularly with regard to the polyesters and related products.
Incidentally, I should like to get together with the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi because the statistics I have on employment in the industry differ from those he quoted. In any event, proportionately there was exactly the same percentage of lay-offs in the United States in the year 1973-74 as in Canada. In other words, there was a general recession brought about primarily by the oil prices of 1973; so many of these products have a petroleum base that large inventories were built up world-wide as a hedge against anticipated problems. These did not materialize to the extent expected and there was subsequently, therefore, a sharp decline in production and sales. To a large extent, that situation has now ironed itself out and here in Canada a recovery is in progress in most sectors. Indeed, some are working at effective capacity, so the picture is not one entirely without promise. I have already mentioned the double-knits; I want to see what we can do about the materials used in these.
There is increased capacity in certain low-cost countries which produce garments, and this has resulted in increased pressure from imports, for example in the area of men's suits, shirts, and outerwear. In all those categories, action has been taken by the Textile and Clothing Board. Virtually all the low-cost countries from which we import are subject to some form of quota. The only case in which we have not gone as far as the board has suggested relates to certain types of outerwear, and we have placed these under surveillance to determine from which country these garments are coming so that we may consider in realistic terms what quota arrangements might be necessary. Only last week, for example, we put a global quota on work

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry
gloves. A whole range of other finished goods and materials is already subject to quota. Thus I do not think it is fair to say that no action has been taken or that public servants have not moved as quickly as possible when crises develop.
I do not, however, deny the legitimacy of the claim that the process is on the slow side. I have looked into this and asked that once a report comes in from the Clothing and Textile Board there should be no delay in taking appropriate action. In this connection I am faced with something of a dilemma. We could table the report quite quickly after it is received from the board, but the policy has been to hold off publication of the report until a decision has been made on the action to be taken.
I notice the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) is laughing. My point is that if we table the report without announcing simultaneously a decision as to the action to be taken, a whole new series of representations might be generated, and this might delay the process still further. For the present we think it advisable to receive the report, decide on a course of action, and then make an announcement accordingly. If hon. members believe a variation in that procedure would spend up the process I would be glad to hear their views.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi made some comments about studies. While this is not my first line of attack on any problem, I might tell him that we do have a study under way at the present time at the request of the parties concerned. Incidentally, I have appointed a union representative to the committee for the first time. The group to which I refer has instructions to report by the end of this month and its terms of reference, together with the preamble, might be worth reading.
In the light of representations that have been received to the effect that:
(a)	the Canadian market for textiles and clothing continues to be severely disrupted by imports,
(b)	there is a need for improvement in the administration of the import control elements of the textile policy, and,
(c)	the currently employed "selective" approach to special measures of protection against "low-cost" imports is ineffective,
it has been decided to form an ad hoc committee composed of three senior executives from the Canadian primary textile industry, three from the Canadian apparel industry, one representative from each of the provinces of Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec, the Assistant Deputy Minister, Industry Development and the Assistant Deputy Minister, International Trade Relations of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Committee will be chaired by the Senior Assistant Deputy Minister, Operations, of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
The mandate of this committee shall be to:
(1)	review current conditions and prospects in the textile and clothing industries and in their market situation,
(2)	review the administration of the policy in relation to import competition,
(3)	examine the appropriateness, given existing legislation and instruments, of implementing the policy in terms of Articles 3 and 4 of the Arrangement Regarding International Trade in Textiles and Article XIX of the G.A.T.T.,
(4)	report its findings and recommendations to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce not later than June 30,1976.
This committee, I am informed, is working very effectively and is considered likely to come up with firm recommendations for immediate implementation. I have no hesitation in saying that I am prepared to move quickly once

some consensus is reached as to what the appropriate action ought to be.
There are many other issues I could discuss if there were sufficient time. One of the things I should like to mention is the whole question of our attitude toward so-called emerging countries. I agree that we must do, as indeed we are doing, a commendable job as Canadians in relating to those countries. I have said to them as recently as March of this year, in the five countries of southeast Asia, that they ought not to think in terms of their industrial development, basing it on such as things as textiles, or one of the problem areas we have, footwear. It will not only make it more difficult for us to be of assistance to them in terms of what they can export to Canada; they will also be competing among themselves in a way which inevitably will be very harmful to their underdeveloped economy.
Having said that, the reality is that for the less developed countries one of the easiest and most labour intensive kinds of activity into which they can move once they start developing economically tends to be textiles. Therefore we have to negotiate with them voluntary quotas in some cases; or, in the last analysis, if they do not work, we must sit down with them and tell them that this is the maximum amount that we are prepared to bring in from a particular country.
Nevertheless we also have to understand and recognize, as one of the committees of the House stated unanimously in a report on international affairs, that we have to provide some kind of access to these countries if we are going to be credible in terms of other things that we are seeking to do internationally. Therefore it is a thin line between protectionism, if you like, in terms of looking after domestic industry, which clearly must be the number one responsibility, and at the same time not talk out of both sides of our mouths at the same time, as it were, when we talk to these undeveloped countries.
I think that up to now we have done a reasonably good job to keep the situation in some kind of balance, particularly, I repeat, since the biggest single source of imports into Canada is still the United States by a very wide margin. There the relationship as to how we work out bilateral agreements, or whatever might be possible under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, is much more difficult and complex than is the case with the less developed world.
While acknowledging that there are major problems in this industry, I have to reject, of course, the idea contained in the motion that virtually nothing is being done and that in some way or other we are allowing a flood of low cost imports to destroy this particular industry. I most emphatically say that whatever may be the case in some sectors of private industry, where I have heard the view expressed, as the hon. member also said, that the textile industry is expendable, I have a complete appreciation of the view expressed by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi that this is an important, indeed essential industry.
It is made all the more so for another reason he mentioned which, by the way, I could broaden beyond his reference to textiles. One of the things that is positively frightening when you contemplate economic development
June 16, 1976

in Canada is the incredible number of one industry towns, not merely textile towns but towns with industries like pulp and paper and mining. The vulnerability of so many of these communities is really a nightmare to contemplate if we do have some kind of across the board slump in some of these rather basic industries, of which of course textiles is one. For that reason, if for no other, it certainly deserves the support not only of the government but of the country.
From what I have said-and I will be glad to provide a detailed list of protectionist (if that is not too strong a word) actions that have been taken-I think it is clear that where there have been identified problem areas some action has been taken, perhaps not as much as the industry might like in some instances, but nevertheless some action has been taken. In terms of this new study, if the global quota turns out to be a more practical approach, then we will look at it seriously. But remember that the basis of the policy, which was endorsed by every member of this House, was against that kind of concept and was based on a high or relatively high tariff, certainly high by today's standard, of about 25 per cent, and selective action on particular commodities or sectors which were giving trouble.
To go to the global quota would be to move completely away from that concept, which I repeat was universally approved of at the time it was introduced about four or five years ago. But if it has to be done, then there is certainly nothing in terms of the laws of the Medes and the Persians about what we have now. We are quite prepared to look at an alternative approach.
I take it that my time is just about up, Mr. Speaker, and I simply want to say that I believe we are taking as well as moving toward some quite decisive actions in the textiles field, and that as the general recovery goes on I hope this will also be reflected in this particular sector, namely, the textile industry.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened to the remarks made by the hon. minister with great interest and I should just like to make one comment. He has on a number of occasions been described as a master of circumlocution, but when it came to his description of how he handles the reports of the textile and clothing board, I really thought he outdid himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, come on. Why don't you give me the answer to the question I asked?

If you listen you will get a few answers.
I rise to take part in this debate for a number of reasons. I first became interested in the problems facing the Canadian textile industry and its synthetic fibres component because it is a major employer in my constituency and the area which surrounds it. But this is not merely an issue of local concern. A number of communities throughout the country are directly affected, and the issue has implications for the secondary manufacturing sector as a whole and for our international trade policy.
The plain fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian textile industry and the associated Canadian fibres industry are in serious trouble. They are losing control of the Canadian market and that has meant and will mean lay-offs, cut-
Textile Industry
backs in capital and research and development investment, a huge trade deficit, and a shift of new investment to the better protected market in the United States.
The causes are complex-competition from countries whose wage levels permit them to undersell domestic manufacturers in the Canadian market, lack of global quotas, and the situation which currently exists in the United States and which has a spillover effect on Canada, to which the minister referred. Something clearly needs to be done.
That is all very well, the doctrinaire free trader may say, but this industry already has tariff protection, anti-dumping laws do exist, some quotas on imports are in place. If these industries are in trouble even with this protection, it is conclusive proof to the doctrinaire free trader that the industry is not competitive in the market place and should be phased out so that the resources allocated to it may be transferred to more productive sectors of the economy. Moreover, he would agree that by opening up our market to imports from Third World countries we not only ensure cheaper prices for the consumer but we assist in the development of those nations' manufacturing sector.
I have heard these arguments repeatedly, and at first hearing they sound very persuasive. Why worry about the demise of the textile industry? To hear this argument one would think its passing would be a national blessing that would, in one fell swoop, bring us a step closer to industrial rationalization, cheaper consumer goods and a fairer distribution of wealth with the developing nations. But it is not quite that simple. We are talking here today about an industry which directly employs 200,000 people, which contributes $5 billion to the Gross National Product, and provides the main economic base for many communities in this country.
Let us be clear about it; we are not talking about the phasing out of an industry as part of some national industrial strategy which will provide alternate employment for its workers and new industries for the communities affected.
