No, indeed, we are talking about an industry which is in danger of being phased out by default. Indeed we are talking about a situation which has developed in large part because the government has failed through procrastination and inertia to take the steps necessary to fulfil the expressed intent of the Canadian textile policy as it was set out in 1970.
Hear, hear!

We have a policy on paper which pledges to create conditions to provide a framework for planning, investment, and development in the industry, and to reverse the decline which it experienced during the 1960's. Yet this policy has been applied with such a lack of conviction, with such procrastination, and in so irresolute a fashion it has disrupted planning, discouraged investment, and cut back on development in the industry. The government vowed to help save the industry, and then has acted as if that expression of its good intentions was sufficient to carry out this difficult and complex task. That simply is not good enough.

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry
A chronic weakness of the government has been that its departments often work at cross purposes to one another. Here we have something even more appalling; a ministry whose implementation of a policy works at cross purposes to the announced intent of that policy.
It is time the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Commerce decided whether or not it wants a strong textile industry in this country, regardless of what the minister had to say this afternoon in his obsequiously expressed concern for the industry. It has to make up its mind whether or not we want a strong textile industry in this country and, if it does, whether it is prepared to take the steps necessary to give that industry a reasonable chance to survive and grow. If it concludes that this industry should be phased out, then let it say so directly and accept the consequences of that decision. If that is what the government intends, let it plan now to cushion the blow to the employees and the communities that will be affected. Let it assess the adverse impact of that step on the balance of trade; let it calculate the effect of that balance of trade deficit on interest rates. Let it investigate the spinoff effects on such related areas as the petro-chemical and synthetic industries. In short, let it cease its present inconsistency between its theory and its practice.
Consistency is the least we should expect, but it is not enough that the government make a decision on this matter. It must make the right decision. In my considered opinion we do need a strong textile industry in Canada. We need it as part of a strong secondary manufacturing sector, both to provide employment and to enhance the strength of the national economy.
Nobody but the most shortsighted nationalist or the most doctrinaire protectionist wants to gouge the consumer to shelter artificial and inefficient industries in this country. But the Canadian textile industry and the synthetic fibre industries associated with it do not fit that stereotype. They are efficient and they are productive. Their annual level of price increase during the past decade is 2 per cent less than that of the manufacturing sector as a whole. Considerable capital investment has been undertaken; $1.7 billion in the last decade, to modernize plant and machinery, and productivity in that decade has gone up 5.1 per cent a year compared to 4.2 per cent for all manufacturing.
The Canadian textile industry is in trouble today not because it is inefficient and unproductive, but because it pays substantially higher wages to its employees than most of its international competitors, and because it is not possible for it to negotiate global quotas. Far from being heavily sheltered or heavily subsidized, the Canadian textile market is relatively wide open. We have only a minuscule part of our market covered by import quotas, 6 per cent as compared to 7 per cent in the United States, and those quotas which amount to only 6 per cent are often shortterm as opposed to the three to five-year import quotas many other countries impose. Moreover, they have to be negotiated item by item for each sector of the industry, a time consuming, complex, and frustrating procedure which places the Canadian textile industry at a great disadvantage compared to other industrialized countries which do utilize the global quota system. The result is that when

some country wants to engage in distress selling, the natural dumping ground is Canada.
Canada is certainly doing its share to provide export opportunities for Third World countries. We hold a smaller percentage of our domestic market than any other country, and that would be the case by a margin of some 15 per cent even if the recommendation of the Senate committee, that 65 per cent of the Canadian market be held for Canadian manufacturers, were accepted without amendment.
I have great sympathy for the cause of economic development in the Third World, and I agree with many of the proposals they put forward at the recent UNCTAD conference in Nairobi, Kenya, to ensure fairer prices for the commodities Third World countries produce. But let us not delude ourselves into thinking that the Canadian market alone is big enough to provide an outlet for all the developing world's textile industries and all of their produce.
If we really want to help these countries, let us work to get the European Economic Community and the United States to open up their textile markets somewhat wider as part of an international agreement. That would be one way in which we could help developing countries. We cannot, as the former minister of industry, trade and commerce said when he brought in the Canadian textile policy in 1970, "assume alone the responsibility for an unliberalized textile world." By attempting to do so we may progressively destroy our own industry while providing only marginal benefits to the developing countries. That is not enlightened compassion, it is senseless sacrifice of a key sector of the national economy of little use to the nations on whose behalf the sacrifice is made.
If we were to abandon every sector of the economy which cannot compete with international competition because of labour costs then we would indeed be embarking on a journey down a slippery slope. Except in a few resource based industries, and those in which transportation costs provide natural protection, we have very few industries in this country which are immune to the plight in which the textile and fibre industries now find themselves.
It used to be that we could overcome labour cost differentials by having better access to technology than the low wage countries, but that advantage is fast disappearing. Let me give you some figures in this regard. In salaries and research facilities, a basic two-person research team composed of a scientist and a technician costs between $65,000 and $90,000 a year. For research and development to be warranted there must be a stable domestic market that will offer the kind of dollar return in business that warrants this expense. But because the textile industry has been losing control of the domestic market, it has cut back on research and development. The situation in my own area illustrates this trend.
Prior to 1970 in Kingston and the Islands and in Fron-tenac-Lennox and Addington there were three Canadian research organizations devoted to the synthetic fibres manufacturing business. Since then Celanese has closed down its Canadian research facilities. DuPont has closed two labs related exclusively to fibres research and has cut
June 16, 1976

its personnel in research and development fibres work by 70 per cent, leaving only some research and development work at its central research facilities in Kingston. All these cutbacks and shutdowns resulted directly from market conditions. In other words, our major competitive advantage, that is, better technology, is being eroded because we are losing control of our market. Surely this is a vicious circle which is of serious national concern.
But the danger goes deeper than that. Technology can now be transferred around the world more and more rapidly. It can be moved at a fairly early stage of its life cycle to lower wage-cost countries. This has special significance to Canada. Because our domestic market is smaller-and the minister referred to this-than that of the United States or the European Economic Community, manufacturing is frequently only warranted several years later than in larger market units. If this market size delay closely corresponds to the time delay in applied technology transferred to lower labour cost situations, then Canada will be in a uniquely disadvantageous position in the future.
We have been discussing the plight of the Canadian textile industry. This is a matter of legitimate and great concern. But the greater concern must be as to whether the same syndrome of drift and indecision on the part of the government will make what is happening to the textile industry a preview of what will happen to the whole of secondary manufacturing enterprise in Canada. That sector is usually one of the more stable elements in our economy. If it goes, we are left with only the resource based industries and the tertiary service sector. More and more we would revert to the colonial-type economy, hewers of wood and drawers of water, which we rejected 100 years ago. More and more we would be dependent on our non-renewable resources to make our way in the world. As a nationalist I cannot consent to that kind of future. The first leader of this country made it his life's work to prevent such a future, and that is one tradition we on this side intend to maintain.
We are paying a price now for moving by default in the direction I have just outlined. Our textile trade deficit last year was $1.1 billion. To balance that outflow of cash Canada is maintaining high interest rates. And with what result? Escalating costs for running the federal and provincial governments and for building roads, schools and hospitals across the country; high interest rates on mortgage loans, and high rents for apartments; unemployment in areas where it is difficult to find alternative employment. The result is that depressed communities and regions in this country will wither and stagnate even more.
Taking all these consequences into consideration we are paying a big price for slightly cheaper clothing and it is symptomatic of a deeper malaise. Through drift, inconsistency, procrastination, and inertia the government is slowly but surely eroding Canada's economic base. There is no challenge to national purpose, and fundamental issues are being treated with bandaids. There can only be one result, Mr. Speaker, national mediocrity. Let us turn away from that road. Let us begin by setting the textile industry in order and let that be the first step toward ensuring the continued growth and development of a strong, efficient, and productive secondary manufacturing sector of which Canadians can be proud.
Textile Industry

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate and to deal with two specific points. First of all, I should like to point out the government's positive record of assistance to the textile industry since May 1970 and secondly, to deal with the present conditions in an important Drummondville textile plant, the Celanese Canada Limited.
With regard to the history of the textile industry in Canada, allow me to briefly recall the following facts: we know that early in 1970, a study of the textile and clothing industry was carried out by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. This study was conducted with the co-operation of other departments concerned after consultation with officials in the industry, the unions and the provincial governments directly involved. The study was undertaken for three main reasons: first, important basic changes in technology, production and demand have created new competitive conditions in those industries in Canada as well as abroad.
Second, the policy designed to settle the problem created by cheap imports had become most difficult to administer, causing undue delays and concerns detrimental to both producers and workers. Third, textile plants, unions and provinces had expressed strong reservations regarding the existing policy in terms of employment and future investments in the industry as well as their impact on regional expansion.
In its review of the situation, the government has taken into consideration the possible contribution of those industries to the whole economy, the need for employment stability, the regional and local implications, the consumer interests, the importance of our export trade and of our international responsibilities. The resulting policy has been set out following the review of the textile and clothing industries. The textile policy has been formally announced by the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, namely the previous representative of my constituency of Drummond, on May 14, 1970. This policy had four main items. First, gradual recovery of the industry towards viable production sectors capable of sustaining ever stronger competition at the international level; second, improvement of legal mechanisms and administrative procedures to deal effectively with the problems of prejudices suffered by Canadian producers because of imports; third, transitional assistance to corporations and workers; fourth, assistance in the areas of technology and marketing.
In the course of the implementation of this policy, the following steps have been taken by the government: The establishment of the Textile and Clothing Board was announced on November 5, 1970 and its three members were appointed on the same date. As everyone knows, the board must make an investigation at the minister's request and it can launch an investigation at the industry's request or on its own. Since its inception, the Textile Board has conducted inquiries on 18 textile and clothing products, for a grand total of 45 inquiries, studies or reviews of these products. Further, it is now looking into two products that were not reviewed previously and reexamining three products that have already been the subject of an inquiry.

Textile Industry
At the present time, eight low cost countries or countries that have nationalized trade are subject to various export restrictions involving 12 products, over and above total restrictions on imports of shirts for men and boys. Other actions have also been taken. A number of programs are being used to help the textile and clothing industries restructure their operations, improve their efficiency and expand their markets. First, from the financial assistance view point, we have the General Adjustment Assistance Program which has been amended to include measures particularly tailored to textile and clothing manufacturers who are now applying their restructuration plan.
Since 1970 44 companies received grants under this program for a total amount of $22 million guaranteed by the government. In addition, 11 companies received grants totalling $45,000 during the same period. Under the Productivity Enhancement Program-PEP-grants covering up to half the cost of feasibility studies were made available to 97 companies for a total amount of $762,000.
Research and development were encouraged: 25 to 30 businesses received assistance every year under the Industrial and Research Development Incentive Act-the IRDIA program. The marketing of products or methods resulting from research work since 1970 brought about expenditures of $2.7 million under PAIT, the Program for Advancement of Industrial Technology.
A second program to promote exports: Canadian companies in the export business received considerable support and produced good results. A third program-manpower training and rehabilitation-and a fourth program-assistance to fashion design-under which millions of dollars were spent by the federal government to help one way or another the textile and clothing industry in Canada. There is also the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. We know that under the Regional Development Incentives Act assented to on July 9, 1969 to promote the creation of productive jobs in designated areas in Canada needing special measures to promote economic development and social progress, textile companies received between 1970 and 1975 grants offers of over $29 million.
Recently, the Senate had a special inquiry, and the minister appeared before the Senate committee. The following points were made: first, that the recent representations made by the industry to the Senate committee as well as to the minister personally contain elements of truth but are not accurate on the whole. It was also determined that when the industry singled out imports from low-cost countries statistics show, as the minister pointed out earlier, that the great majority of imports come from developed countries, particularly the United States. Third, it was shown that imports from low-cost countries are an important factor in the problem as a whole. It was also shown that industry hires a large number of people difficult to retrain. Finally, it was pointed out before that committee that industry showed vision, imagination and that its efforts to rationalize and modernize structures were successful. I am happy with the suggestions of the minister who says that in his opinion the textile industry is essential, that it is an important industrial sector, that he is aware of the legitimate desire of the industry for stability and that he has no thought whatsoever of sacrificing the

textile industry to increase Canadian imports from developing countries.
There was some reference to an ad hoc advisory committee of clothing and textile industries which was recently established. The minister spoke in detail of the mandate of that committee, and I am glad to find out that following my intervention in the House on May 19 last, asking for the representation of employees from the textile sector on this important committee responsible for reviewing the whole textile policy in Canada, this request has been agreed to and the minister confirmed today that spokesmen for textile employees are now members of that important committee so as to express the constructive views of the employees from that important sector of industry who want to protect and keep their jobs.
This leads me to talk about the specific problem now prevailing at Drummondville, in the riding of Drummond which I represent, in the plant of Celanese Canada Limited. The dispute in this plant is no longer a private confrontation between management and labour. More than 1,600 textile workers having been without their regular jobs for several weeks, almost two months now, it is clear that the situation has become dramatic for them, their families and the whole community.
As soon as I was elected member of parliament for Drummond nearly two years ago, I asked local employers to make a special effort to improve employment conditions and wages in a region where wages were among the lowest in Canada. Most businesses in the area reacted well and made an effort, and the situation is now improving. I warmly contratulate all those employers and I thank them for their cooperation.
As concerns the Celanese plant, which is the largest employer in Drummondville, I must say that I am disappointed to see that it does not seem to want to react favourably to my appeal. In view of the constant and increased efforts on the part of the federal government to help the textile industry, as I have just shown, it would be normal that Celanese Canada of Drummondville demonstrate a greater social conscience. This long lockout by Celanese is an insult to the population.
I find it completely unacceptable and scandalous that a multinational company can so deny its responsibilities as good citizen and can betray so arrogantly not only its employees, which make up a high proportion of the local manpower, but also the rest of the population in an area which is desperately trying to increase its low economic growth rate. In view of its importance and of the evolution of Drummondville, this plant should cooperate, offer itself as an example, and consequently, not abuse a right conferred by the Quebec Labour Code. In the present case, this radical position is clearly irrespectful of the rights and qualities of the textile employees who have certainly not been among the best paid workers in the past and who are now nearly defenceless and resourceless.
It is more than time for Celanese to show, as an important citizen of Drummondville, a true social conscience, like it should in a society which wants to be just and needs to renew itself. It is because I am concerned for my constituents' economic and social welfare which is now in danger that I make an urgent appeal to those responsible: 1-for this lockout to stop immediately; 2-for negotiations
June 16, 1976

to take place in good faith and without delay; 3-not Celanese employees to be granted the excellent working conditions that they deserve and that the employer can give them.
I finally succeeded in reaching the general manager of this company last Thursday, June 10, and I asked him to put an end immediately to this lock-out. He told me that he could not then promise me that he would do so in the near future, but that he would talk about it to the other managers and his superiors. Today, June 16, the lockout is still on and nearly 1,600 employees are deprived of their means of subsistence. Incidentally, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate all those, and there are many of them, who make peaceful demonstrations in good faith or who help Celanese employees in other ways. I urge all the population to support morally the employees who are victim of the lockout at Celanese, and I hope that landlords, businessmen and creditors will be patient with those people who are now without any means of support. Those humanitarian gestures can only add to the pride and credit of my fellow citizens.
If, today, for the love of strategy, the big employers want to use lockouts systematically in their fight against big unions, for God's sake let them avoid doing so on the back of the vulnerable textile sector, on the backs of 1,600 workers at Drummondville, and above all, let them choose another battlefield than a city like Drummondville where efforts are being made to improve the low rate of economic growth. My stand, in view of the circumstances, is definitely not incompatible with the spirit of the anti-inflation act and its regulations, quite the contrary.
The Celanese Company at Drummondville which employs, as we know, over 500 employees, benefits from the exception provided by the act. The workers' contract was signed before January 1, 1974. In addition, the contract expired some time in April 1975, that is before the antiinflation act became effective on October 14, 1975. Consequently, in view of the act and resulting regulations, and especially regulation No. 44, the Celanese workers are considered exceptions and are not limited to 12 per cent salary increases; so they can negotiate without any ceiling; when an agreement is reached with the employer for an increase of 18 per cent, 25 per cent or more this agreement must be submitted to the Anti-Inflation Board for approval. The board can endorse the agreement as submitted or change it; if it does change it there is an opportunity to appeal since an amendment was made recently to the Anti-Inflation Act.
As we can see, a special consideration criterion applies to labour groups who signed their last contract before January 1, 1974 if that contract expired before October 14, 1975 and a new contract was not signed before October 14, 1975. In other words those contracts were signed before the fast escalation of the cost of living that started in 1974. So protection is given to those employee groups like those of Celanese in Drummondville.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) who restated today the importance of the textile sector of the industry and who declared to be ever more prepared to support that industry. I thank him for heeding my intervention in the House of Commons on May 19, 1976 and
Textile Industry
allowing the spokesmen for textile workers to participate in the important ad hoc committee responsible for reviewing the whole textile policy in Canada and presenting a report before June 30.
I for one intend to continue to fight fiercely for the improvement of the textile and clothing industry situation in Canada and I do not intend to stop making interventions in the House of Commons as I have been doing in the last two years and particularly on November 18, 1974, November 28, 1974 and May 19, 1976. I wish to continue interventions like those I made one month ago before the regional economic expansion committee to get better wages for textile employees through subsidies from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to the textile and clothing industry in Canada. I intend to have more meetings like those I had last year with representatives of all textile industries in Canada, here in Ottawa, and the many other meetings I have had in the two last years with textile employee representatives here in Ottawa or elsewhere in my riding. Lastly, I wish that Celanese Canada Limited revise immediately its radical strategy in Drummondville, as I asked earlier, in the interest of the people I have the honour to represent.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be glad to make some remarks on a subject which is so important and, having heard a few speeches, I am deeply convinced that some hon. members are really interested in this problem. I would like to congratulate in particular all my colleagues who agreed to take this day to discuss this subject, because we recognize the importance of this industry. I extend special words of praise to my colleague the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) who made some very interesting remarks.
At the same time I listened to the minister who himself attempted to prove that it is not a matter of ill will, but it would seem that answers and solutions are not forthcoming today. Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw your attention to the absence of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) who told me he would have been really pleased to take part in this debate but he is out of the country with a parliamentary committee. He is particularly concerned for the workers of his riding.
Other members have dealt with the hardships faced by the textile workers in their respective regions. Well, I wish as well to refer to those of my own region, and to a large city of my riding in particular, the city of Joliette. As everywhere else, claims have been made there both by the management and the unions, and for several years, even though it has been emphasized that since 1970 the government has made special efforts for the recovery of this area for the benefit of this class of workers. It seems that the effects are not as yet being felt and consequently, in Canada as everywhere else, there has been a drastic cut in two industries of my riding: their staff have been reduced from 210 to 160 and from 75 to 20 respectively.
Mr. Speaker, imports seem to be one of the major issues. I could not miss this opportunity to make a few comments to urge the government to take more efficient action than was taken in recent years.

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry
I know, Mr. Speaker, there are some commercial trade agreements. We all know that but we wonder, and rightly so, whether the government should not attempt to secure Canadian production. In my view, it is important to secure at least this minimum requirement which the people concerned and even the unions have discussed with the responsible minister and the board. They have met the representatives of the political parties and the unions expect a minimum of production in the textile industry and its by-products.
I suggest that it is important to remind the government that it is vital to maintain a minimum of our Canadian production, made by Canadians and for Canadians. It would be dangerous and we know it too well, as the same thing is happening in other areas, to see that the Canadian people are under the obligation to buy foreign products. We have seen the aftermath of such a situation in the oil industry, and we will see it in other areas. Because of the lack of a well-defined policy, we will have to rely on foreign products and God knows what price we will have to pay then.
Therefore, even if it raises some difficulties, I believe it is important for the government to commit itself to support the industry, and the textile industry in particular, to encourage it, to attempt to find proper remedies and to have the courage to impose the necessary controls unless we are prepared to see it disappear on a national scale. In brief, Mr. Speaker, this must be our goal.
We on this side of the House could accuse the government and limit our debate to these accusations but we know that since 1970 the government has shown an interest in this matter. But one thing for sure, Mr. Speaker, even if the government does its best, what is happening? If some hon. members claim that the government did find solutions we still are in a difficult position and the textile industry workers are far from being satisfied: employees, management, members of the unions and union leaders alike. What is clear is that the actions of the government and the investigation committees have unfortunately taken much too long in providing us with the analyses and giving us the appropriate answers.
It is clear that the situation is deteriorating and that things are getting tough not only in the textile industry but in many other areas. So, the question we should ask ourselves is what sort of economic performance can the government offer the country? That is the whole question. Recently, Mr. Speaker, we had the visit of thousands of milk producers. We had hundreds and hundreds of workers from all walks of life over the last few years. Today, we are dealing with one topic: textile. The government has been saying for a decade that it will improve this area and find solutions. It set up commissions yet no one is satisfied. I personally believe that the government has lacked the courage to implement the controls which are necessary to save a Canadian industry. They may boast about and point at the massive investments poured by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion into several industries, I still think that we had better first preserve those which exist already. And when an important class of workers is allowed to be dismissed, are we sure we are in a position to recycle them for other fields? Those are questions that we must ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker?

Therefore, from the discussions we are having today, it is obvious that we do not have the power to solve the problem, but we believe that as representatives of our constituents and considering that those 250,000 workers are deeply concerned as are the owners who invested heavily, it is our duty to press the government into taking more effective measures. We hope that we will be able today to point out specifically those difficulties and entice the government to consider them more carefully and to find solutions, which is their reponsibility. The government has the power to administer this country and to find the required solutions.
In view of the lack of satisfactory measures, are we allowed to think that the government has run out of possibilities to create and find the initiatives that are required? We ask ourselves certain questions, precisely about that absence of reasonable and necessary solutions.
Mr. Speaker, I know that some of my colleagues wish to take the floor after me and I will limit myself to these comments, and refrain from repeating certain statistics already put on record by other speakers. But I dare hope that we can straighten out one point in particular, whenever mention is made of a Canadian trade balance showing a deficit of some $875 million in the field of textile alone. This shows, I believe, a special lack of interest for that industry.
Under the circumstances, and taking in account those problems and the representations made by the representatives and the union workers particularly involved, I would believe that the government will listen more carefully still; and I would like also to point out that recently unions were able to have a discussion with the minister and the Commission. The member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard) has pointed out earlier that it was most interesting to note that the minister has seen the need to invite union representatives in order to discuss such important and alarming issues.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I hope that this day will have well served the interests of this class of workers and I hope that the government will respond more efficiently than he did today. While recognizing the good will of the minister, I believe that the desire and the efforts of the government, if there were any, were clearly inadequate. Should the workers and industry owners be asked that question?
Let me go back to this objective, which I feel is essential, that is to save our Canadian industry and to maintain a domestic production for Canadians; the government in that area will have to do something more significant and more effective than whatever he has done up to now.

Mr. Speaker, I, with others in the House, am indebted to the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Balfour) for the opportunity to debate this important subject. I am indebted to all who participated in the debate not only for their contributions but also for observing the time limit on speeches. I am particularly indebted to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) who preceded me for limiting his remarks. I shall try to finish before six o'clock, to allow one more government

June 16, 1976

spokesman the opportunity to speak. I understand that an hon. member opposite wishes to make a few remarks.
I,	and I suppose most of my colleagues in the House, always enjoy hearing the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) speak; this afternoon was no exception. But I know that others share my view when I say that this afternoon the minister's remarks lacked conviction. I was disappointed by his speech, disappointed because the minister used as an excuse the fact he was getting conflicting views from within the industry. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) likes to use a similar phrase, which is without validity.
I suggest that if the minister is getting conflicting views from within the industry the fault lies solely with our selective import policy. Inevitably, if the government is to impose selective tariffs and controls, it will obtain conflicting views from within the industry. Each manufacturer in the industry, whether he manufacturers yarn, fibre or finished goods, will want to look after himself and his employees. Therefore if the government pursues a policy involving selective controls or tariffs, it should not be surprised when it receives conflicting views from the industry.
I agree that originally the present policy was initiated with the blessing of hon. members in all parts of the House. But the policy has not worked.
I was also disappointed by the way the minister used statistics, supplied presumably by his department; I was disappointed to hear him talk about the textile industry in terms of dollars, when for generations the output of the industry has not been measured in dollars but in pounds of yarn, or the equivalent. Therefore it did the minister no credit when quoting statistics to speak in terms of dollars and cents. Perhaps his departmental officials are at fault; I do not care. That industry's production has always been measured in pounds, and the measurement has not changed. Let us speak properly in this debate and talk in terms of pounds.
There is no question in the minister's mind about the serious condition of the textile industry. He and I may disagree about the degree of seriousness. Be that as it may, we on my side of the House think this is a matter of extreme urgency and attach great importance to any proposals for solving the difficulties of the industry.
Hon. members have spoken of volumes of production and the percentage of the domestic market served by domestic producers. I do not think there was much discrepancy between the figures the minister used and those used by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). I have always used the same statistics to which the minister referred, statistics which were tabled in the standing committee. They show that we have gone from the position where we supplied 64 per cent of our domestic market in 1964 to a position of supplying but 46 per cent in 1975. That drop in itself is alarming. But it is all the more alarming when we compare figures for this country with those pertaining to our trading partners. I believe that the United States industry supplies 88 per cent of its domestic market, and in Common Market countries, indigenous industries supply about 80 per cent of those markets. The statistics concerning pounds of production are enough to
Textile Industry
alarm anyone. They show how serious the situation has become; it warrants immediate consideration.
I do not quarrel about the establishment of the ad hoc committee but agree with the minister; the mere establishment of a committee will not lead, inevitably, to the solution of the serious difficulty. I appreciate the minister's frankness in saying that while he respects the committee and looks forward to a report he does not think it will solve the problem. Hopefully the committee will make the extent of the problem clearer. No industry in Canada has been subjected to more surveys, questionnaires, investigations, and reports than the poor textile industry. I would hate, as a manufacturer of textiles, to face tomorrow morning yet another inquiry into by business. I think the industry is sick and tired of this procedure. I think the same can be said for that part of the industry based in Quebec. I do not think conditions in the textile industry in Quebec are much different.
I know the difficulties large textile manufacturers face in creating the basis of the economic life of their communities. Most of the members of the association in my part of Ontario, myself included, are manufacturers who employ, generally, fewer than 100 people. Usually our manufacturers are located in small, rural-oriented communities and provide a small but firm but economic base for those communities. I wish to express my concern on behalf of those people.
In terms of employment in the whole industry, I do not think the statistics need too much elaboration. Forty-six per cent of the domestic market employs roughly 200,000 people, according to statistics I have received. That means for each 1 per cent of the market we have we provide roughly 4,350 Canadians with jobs. Seventy-five per cent of the market would result in an increase of roughly 125,000 positions within that industry. At the Senate committee it was clear that the minister felt that Canada could not expect to supply 75 per cent of its domestic requirements. He may be right, but I am not prepared to agree to that point.
When one talks about employment in the textile industry it is often discouraging when one hears the accusation that this is a low paying industry. I have to reject that. It may have been historically true. I do not know. My first job as a 12-year old student was in a textile plant. I think I got 33 cents an hour, which was pretty good pay in those days.
In terms of current industry I notice that we pay substantially higher than, for example, the United States. In terms of productivity, it is extremely serious in terms of economic conditions today when an industry is failing to produce to its capacity, or reasonably approaching its capacity. The lack of reaching capacity is as equally inflationary as increased prices and wages. In other words, if we are losing the potential to contribute to our Gross National Product, that is equally as inflationary as substantial pay increases or price hikes. Therefore in terms of an entire industry, if Canadian textiles are producing at roughly 60 or 70 per cent of existing plant capacity, we are contributing that loss of potential to the inflationary pressures besetting our economy.

June 16, 1976
Textile Industry
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi mentioned the potential loss of this entire industry. The minister says that is simply not true. I do not doubt his word. However, certainly many of those in the industry perceive this to be government policy. That is terribly serious, particularly for a small businessman. If he perceives that government policy is such as to permit the eventual elimination of the industry, whether his perception is right or wrong, there is no possible way that he is going to make capital investment in his company either to create more jobs to maintain a satisfactory level of efficiency or to increase his production. Therefore I say to the minister that while that may not be the policy, and while he was very clear on that, that is the perception among many in the industry. The fact that that perception exists is in itself a very serious matter.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi talked about what would happen if we lost an industry and were at the mercy of exporting countries. I have been through that with regard to baler twine, which was also mentioned. It is a simple fact of life.
Those who have spoken have touched briefly on the relations between the department and the industry. Again, it may be a fact or it may be a perception-to me, it makes absolutely no difference-those in the textile industry perceive their relations with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce as confrontation. Whether that perception is correct or incorrect, it matters not. If that is a broadly accepted fact by those in the industry, it is an extremely serious matter. Those in the industry believe they are not being consulted. They believe they are not being consulted before trade negotiations take place. If that is a fact, and frankly I believe that it is, the minister has a very serious problem within his department. I wish him well in the solution of that problem. I do not want him in any way to minimize how strongly small businessmen, at least those I know, feel that they are in a continual confrontation program with the department. That is not the minister's nature and I urge him to direct his mind to that particular problem which exists among people in the textile industry.
We have been talking about tariffs today. I suggest they are not the answer. In my opinion, many of them have been simple window dressing. The eventual answer has to be quotas. They have to be global. It has to be comprehensive. I do not know what other way to approach the matter.
The minister is considering that. I look forward to his remarks following the report of the ad hoc committee at the end of this month. The minister knows the problems. They are set out in the preamble to the terms of reference of the ad hoc committee. The first deals with the import situation. I know that we import from both developing countries and the United States. I know the share the United States has in the market. I know and accept as a fact that the minister has warned the developing countries they cannot continue indefinitely at this level. I acknowledge, as the minister said, that we have international obligations and a fine line to walk.
What impressed me about the testimony in the Senate committee, and I wish he had said it today, is that we should be thinking more in terms of exporting expertise to these developing countries. There are trade commissioners who have retired, and I believe that is one example the

minister gave before the Senate committee. We should have been doing this for years in agriculture. Instead we played the role of Lady Bountiful and handed out a few million here and a few million there, without making any effort to make the developing countries self sufficient. I agree that instead of increasing our import levels from them, it is equally important to send them that expertise, whether it be in agriculture, industry, urban affairs, or fighting pollution. I encourage the minister to develop that particular line of thought and that particular policy.
With respect to our self sufficiency and reliance on other countries, the department is prepared to accept that Canada may not be self sufficient, if I read the evidence correctly in the transcript of the Senate hearings. I do not know why it accepts that. I become terribly discouraged when I see how counterproductive the DREE program in relation to the textile industry have become-and the minister is very familiar with this-in the Maritimes. People from Ontario and Quebec went into the Maritimes when those businesses failed and picked up machinery and inventories at bargain prices. I know how discouraging that must have been. I make this as a personal observation.
I urge the minister to consider developing some form of short-term freeze, and I mean by that three, four or five years, on the level of imports. He set the groundwork by warning the developing countries about this in order to give the industry a gradual opportunity to increase to a reasonable level its share of the domestic market. I think the minister can do that without betraying our international obligations and without an adverse effect on the consumer. I would give the industry an opportunity, which is so important to it, to plan its capital investment for the future.
I realize that may be a rather dramatic action. It may not be as easy as a stroke of the pen saying we are freezing imports at current levels. However, I urge the minister to consider that one short term approach to this problem. It would certainly give the industry some confidence in the sincerity of the government in so far as its problems are concerned.
The second item in the preamble to the terms of reference of the ad hoc committee is better administration of those import control elements that we now have. I suggest the mechanics are there. I believe the Textile Institute has said frankly to the minister, "Yes, you have the mechanics; We are satisfied with what you have; It is just the way you are implementing the system." The minister has acknowledged that the system is too slow.
The other day I got a list of references made this year to the Textile and Clothing Board. The date of the brief regarding acrylic yarn was January 6, the report was made on February 11, and the public announcement on April 14. A brief in connection with sweaters was submitted on January 19. No report has been issued. Nylon and polyester fabrics, March 15, no report; worsted fabrics, April 5, no report; knit fabrics, May 7, no report; polyester yarn and hosiery, updating of reports earlier released-I do not know the date of the brief.
Another aspect of the subject is this: when some form of control is imposed, what measures do we take to enforce it?
June 16, 1976

I suggest to the minister that while we have the necessary mechanism at our disposal we do nothing to enforce it. On the other hand, when the authorities in our neighbour to the south hear of a ship halfway between Taiwan and the U.S. carrying a cargo the discharge of which would breach the control measures established by the United States, that ship is directed not to unload those goods at a U.S. port. The whole world knows that this is U.S. policy, and that is why it is so effective.
The third item in the preamble has to do with the present "selective" approach to special measures of protection against low-cost imports and the suggestion that it is ineffective. I mentioned this earlier. I cannot agree that the prohibition of the entry of fabrics solves anything when one may import the yarn on the one hand and the finished product on the other. My view is that, unhappily, the present approach has not worked. It is obviously not the approach taken by the United States or by the Common Market. Unfortunately, although I agree it received the approval of all concerned, it has not proved to be effective enough.
I wish the committee well in its deliberations. I look forward to its report at the end of the month. In conclusion I think I can do no better than quote the minister, if he will forgive my bad manners. This is what he said in another committee:
There is no view anywhere in the government that the textile industry is dispensable. It is an important industrial segment in Canada and it is our intention to do whatever is possible to give it a degree of viability.
In that regard I completely support the minister's position. But I have not seen him put his money where his mouth is to this date.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened closely to the suggestions made by opposition members, and I have taken some notes. I was somewhat amazed to see the phrasing of the motion introduced by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). As the minister stated at the beginning of his speech, when the phrasing and the remarks by the hon. member from Brome-Missisquoi are considered, and this is literal, he supported the federal textile and clothing policy.
Overall, I believe he mentioned twice he was satisfied with the current textile and clothing policy. However, some other members referred to the possibility of reviewing the level of imports, and some referred to the need for certain protectionist measures. In my view, the textile situation is not as gloomy as certain would have it or would imply, as the minister indicated. I suggest the goals are quite clear and the minister stated he was about the textile industry, a vital one in Canada. This was an important segment of manufacturing industry, and he was aware of that industry's hope for stable employment. I think that these points are made up of basic points excessively impor-
Textile Industry
tant for the employers and especially the employees of the textile industries. One of these is that we should not sacrifice the textile industry to increase our imports from developing countries. Again, I think this is an excessively important point. Mr. Speaker, everybody makes reference to figures or statistics and I could follow along on this line because everybody here says that everything depends on the basis chosen for the comparisons, whether they are made on a money, pound or shipping basis. By the way, from 1970 to 1975, our clothing exports increased by 44 per cent. During the same period, our textile exports increased by 34 per cent.
So everything depends on the figures and the comparisons which we want to make. There is one point which has not been raised today-and I think it should be-it is that we should promote some kind of enthusiasm within the consumers. We should develop some kind of advertising campaign to incite the consumers to buy made-in-Canada products. I think that this point is extremely important even if we ask that protectionist measures be taken and, here again, all kinds of solutions may be proposed but I think it is necessary to create a certain feeling in Canada so that in the stores the Canadian consumer may buy and demand products made in Canada. I think this is extremely important and if each one of us behaves according to his own conscience, we could see how we could bring our own excessively imprtant solution if we really believe in this industry.
I made my own experience, I do not know much about the textile industry but, considering my new responsibilities, each weekend I try to go either to a shopping centre or to a department store to see how many products made in Canada I can find; I realize that there are many but that, here again, Canadians themselves are not aware of the purchasing potential they represent to promote the textile and clothing industries in Canada.

An increased willingness to buy Canadian would be one element in the solution of that problem.

Mr. Speaker, it is the last contribution to this debate which seemed to me very useful. The minister detailed all the various policies being applied and I think that a report prepared by an ad hoc committee with representatives from the three provinces, the manufacturing industry and department officials will soon be tabled. The minister indicated also that the unions will take part in that committee which will review the whole textile and clothing policy and which is expected to produce a report on that question before June 30.

It being six o'clock, it is my duty to inform the House that pursuant to Standing Order 58(11) proceedings under the motion have expired.
It being six o'clock, the House stands adjourned until Thursday at 11 a.m., pursuant to special order of Monday, June 7.

Thursday, June 17, 1976
